title: Transcription That Knows Your Jargon and Deletes Your 'Ums'
hook: Google's new Gemini 3.5 Transcribe handles more than 85 languages, picks up specialized vocabulary on its own, and quietly cleans the filler words out of what you said.
key_points: Gemini 3.5 Transcribe covers more than 85 languages and auto-detects specialized jargon, per The Verge.
It strips filler like 'um' and 'ah', producing text that reads cleaner than the audio sounded.
The same model powers Gboard's Rambler feature and is rolling into more Google products, including Chrome.
Accurate jargon handling is what made older dictation tools useless for medicine, law, and engineering.
A tidied transcript is an edited transcript — fine for notes, riskier as a record of what someone said.
content_html: Google has added a transcription model to the Gemini family: Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Per The Verge, it covers more than 85 languages, automatically recognizes specialized jargon without being told the domain in advance, and tidies your speech as it goes — the "ums" and "ahs" don't make it into the text. Ars Technica notes it's the same technology behind Gboard's Rambler dictation, now spreading into more Google products including Chrome.
extra_html:
The jargon part is the genuinely useful advance. Anyone who has tried to dictate a medical note, a legal clause, or a list of part numbers into older software knows the failure mode: the everyday words come out fine and every term you actually needed comes out mangled. A model that picks up domain vocabulary on its own is the difference between a transcript you edit for ten minutes and one you throw away. Alongside 3.5 Live Translate, it also points at where this is heading — audio as a first-class input, not a novelty feature.

One small habit worth keeping. A transcript that deletes filler is an edited transcript. For meeting notes or a first draft, that's a gift. For anything where the record matters — an interview, a dispute about what was promised, a source quote — remember that the polish is the model's, not the speaker's, and keep the original audio.

related.title: Voice Assistants
related.hook: Siri and Alexa could set a timer; the new voice AIs can hold a real conversation. Talking is becoming a normal way to use AI — handy, natural, and always a little bit listening.

related.title: AI & Accessibility
related.hook: For people with disabilities, AI is often life-changing: apps that describe the world to blind users, caption speech for deaf users, or give a synthetic voice back to someone who lost theirs.

related.title: Breaking Language Barriers
related.hook: AI translation has gone from comically bad to genuinely useful — text, speech, even live signs through your camera. Good enough to travel and connect; not yet good enough for the contract.

flashcards.prompt: What makes automatic jargon detection a big deal for transcription?

choices.text: Specialized vocabulary is where older dictation tools failed hardest
It lets the model transcribe faster than real time
It removes the need for a microphone

flashcards.explanation_html: Medical, legal, and technical terms were the classic breaking point for dictation software. Getting them right is what makes a transcript usable at work.

flashcards.prompt: Why should you be a little careful with a transcript that removes filler words?
flashcards.back_html: It's a cleaned-up version, not a verbatim record. Great for notes and drafts; less appropriate where exactly what someone said, hesitations included, matters.
